explanations.answer: An upper room where they're staying
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Acts 1:13 says they went to the upper room where they were staying. They came back to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives (Acts 1:12) and went to a room with a little altitude. I respect any room that comes with altitude.

explanations.answer: The house of Simon the tanner
explanations.explanation: Simon the tanner is a real man in Acts, but he's in a different spot. Peter stays with him in Joppa, a coastal town (Acts 9:43). In this passage, the apostles go to an upper room in Jerusalem. Different city, different host, but nice memory for names, friend.

Gethsemane is where Jesus went with His disciples to pray before His arrest (Matthew 26:36). That's a different night in a different story. Here, after leaving the Mount of Olives, they return to Jerusalem and go to the upper room where they were staying (Acts 1:12-13). They're going indoors this time, with a roof.

Eleven is right. Count them off: Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James. That Judas is a different man from the one Peter talks about later. One chair in the circle is empty, and that's what this whole passage is about.

I get why you'd say twelve, since twelve is the number people expect. But the list in Acts 1:13 has eleven names, and I counted twice with my mustache. Someone is missing from the group, and Peter gets to that in a minute. Hang on to the number twelve, because it comes back.

Ten is close, but the list has one more name than that. Start with Peter and John and go all the way to Judas son of James, and you land on eleven. Easy to drop one in that long string of names. I do the same thing when I count cookies off the cooling rack, and the last one hides behind the spatula.

Prayer is the word. Acts 1:14 says, “With one accord they all continued in prayer…” Notice the words "With one accord…" They're all stirring the same bowl in the same direction. And they keep at it. They continue.

Hiding makes sense as a guess, since they're in a room upstairs. But the text doesn't say they're hiding. It says they all continued in prayer with one accord (Acts 1:14). I'd rather tell you what the verse says than guess at what's in their heads.

Fasting is a real thing people do in the Bible, but this verse doesn't mention it. What Acts 1:14 says is that they all continued in prayer. When the text names one thing, I let it name that one thing. Prayer is the answer here, baker.

explanations.answer: Mary the mother of Jesus and His brothers
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Acts 1:14 says they prayed “…along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with His brothers.” So the room is bigger than just the eleven. It's a full house, and everybody in it is praying.

explanations.answer: Lazarus and his sisters Mary and Martha
explanations.explanation: Lazarus, Mary and Martha are a real family. Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead (John 11:43-44). But Acts 1:14 doesn't list them here. It names Mary the mother of Jesus and His brothers, along with the women. Good guess, friend, those are names worth remembering.

Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea take care of Jesus's body after the cross (John 19:38-39). Acts 1:14 doesn't put them here, though. The verse names Mary the mother of Jesus and His brothers. Good guess, friend, those are names worth remembering.

Right on. Acts 1:15 says it was “a gathering of about a hundred and twenty…” That's a lot of people standing around while Peter stands up. And notice it says "about," so I won't claim it's an exact headcount.

Five hundred is a number that shows up elsewhere in Scripture. Paul, an apostle, writes that Jesus appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time (1 Corinthians 15:6). But in this scene, Acts 1:15 says about a hundred and twenty. Different gathering, different count.
Seventy is a nice round number, but it's not the one in this verse. Acts 1:15 says the gathering was about a hundred and twenty. I'd have needed a few extra trays for that many people.
Arrested is right. Peter says Judas “…became a guide for those who arrested Jesus.” (Acts 1:16) Peter is stating what Judas did, and he says it plainly. It's a sad line, and I think Peter knows it.

Crucified is a heavy word, and I see why it came to mind. But Peter's words in Acts 1:16 are that Judas became a guide for those who arrested Jesus. The verse stops at the arrest. That's what Peter says, so that's what we'll say.

Followed is a good word, and Judas did walk with Jesus's group. Peter says in the next verse, “He was one of our number and shared in this ministry.” (Acts 1:17) But verse 16 uses a different word for what Judas guided people to do: arrest Jesus. Keep reading these verses side by side, baker.
This one's false, baker. Peter says the opposite: “He was one of our number and shared in this ministry.” (Acts 1:17) Judas really was in the group. That's part of what makes this passage so heavy.

False is right. Peter says, “He was one of our number and shared in this ministry.” (Acts 1:17) Judas wasn't an outsider. He was counted with them and shared in the work. I think that's why this part is so sad.

Blood is right. Acts 1:19 says the people in Jerusalem called the field Akeldama in their own language, that is, Field of Blood. I think this part of the story is heavy. We'll let it be heavy and move on gently.

Mercy is a lovely word, and I can see why you reached for it. But the name in Acts 1:19 is Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood. The text gives the name the people used. This one's a sad spot in the story, baker.

Silver is a natural word to reach for, baker, but it isn't in this verse. The name of the field, Akeldama, means Field of Blood (Acts 1:19). Acts 1:18 says Judas bought the field with the reward for his wickedness. I think this verse hurts a little, and it's okay to feel that.

True! Peter quotes two lines from the book of Psalms. The second one is “May another take his position.” (Acts 1:20) So there's an empty position that someone else can fill. That's where the story turns next.

Hold on, baker, this one's true. After quoting “May his place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in it…” Peter adds another line from Psalms: “May another take his position.” (Acts 1:20) That second line is about someone else taking Judas's position. Nice try, though.

explanations.answer: From John the Baptist's baptism until Jesus was taken up
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Peter says the man must have been with them “…beginning from John’s baptism until the day Jesus was taken up from us.” (Acts 1:22) That's a long stretch of time, and he's got to have been there for all of it. Missing a few weeks of the show wouldn't count.

explanations.answer: From the wedding at Cana until the cross
explanations.explanation: The wedding at Cana is a real moment in Jesus's ministry (John 2:1-11), so I see where that came from. But Peter doesn't name it, and he doesn't stop at the cross. He says from John's baptism until the day Jesus was taken up (Acts 1:22). A longer span than you'd guess.

explanations.answer: From the Sermon on the Mount until the tomb
explanations.explanation: The Sermon on the Mount is in Matthew 5, and it's a great place to look. But Peter doesn't start there, and he doesn't end at the tomb. He says the new man must have been with them from John's baptism until the day Jesus was taken up (Acts 1:22). That's the whole stretch.
True, baker. Peter says, “For one of these must become a witness with us of His resurrection.” (Acts 1:22) A witness tells what he saw. And what he has to tell is that Jesus rose.

Close, but this is true. Peter says “For one of these must become a witness with us of His resurrection.” (Acts 1:22) The new man is to be a witness with them. And what he'll bear witness to is Jesus's resurrection.

They pray, yes. Acts 1:24 says, “And they prayed…” and then they ask the Lord to show them which of the two He has chosen. Two names are on the table, and they take it to the Lord. I do the same before I open the oven.

Calling in the elders sounds sensible, friend. I'd probably schedule a meeting about the meeting. But the text doesn't mention any elders being sent for. After they propose the two men, Acts 1:24 says they prayed.

explanations.answer: They let the two men speak
explanations.explanation: Letting each man speak sounds fair, and I'd probably want a speech or two myself. But the passage never says either man spoke. What it does say is that they prayed (Acts 1:24). Prayer is what's on the page, so that's where I'm staying, baker.
Heart is the word. They pray, “Lord, You know everyone’s heart. Show us which of these two You have chosen” (Acts 1:24) They ask the One who knows hearts to show them. That's the whole request.
Name is a natural guess, since names were just listed. But the prayer says, “Lord, You know everyone’s heart.” (Acts 1:24) It's the heart they say He knows. And that's what they're counting on.
Past is a fair guess, friend. But their prayer says, “Lord, You know everyone’s heart.” (Acts 1:24) They name the heart, not the past. It's a small difference, but it's the one the text uses.
This is false, baker. Acts 1:26 says, “Then they cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias.” There's no vote mentioned in the text. They pray, they cast lots, and the lot falls.
False is right. The text doesn't mention a vote. It says, “Then they cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias.” (Acts 1:26) Nobody's raising a hand or counting ballots in this passage.

Matthias it is. “Then they cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias. So he was added to the eleven apostles.” (Acts 1:26) That's the whole decision, in one verse. And now there's a twelfth chair filled.

Justus is the other man. Acts 1:23 says they proposed Joseph called Barsabbas, who's also known as Justus, and Matthias. The lot fell to Matthias, not Justus (Acts 1:26). One man, two names, and he didn't get picked this time.

Silas didn't make the list, friend. The text gives two names: Joseph called Barsabbas, also known as Justus, and Matthias (Acts 1:23). The lot fell to Matthias (Acts 1:26). Silas can't win a lot he was never put into.
